entry.title: A crash and a corrupt disk look the same
entry.summary: How NodusDB's log tells a power cut from a damaged disk, built from what write and fsync really promise, and what 2,858 simulated crashes did and did not prove.
entry.content:
How NodusDB's log tells a power cut from a damaged disk, built from what write and fsync really promise, and what 2,858 simulated crashes did and did not prove.

Every database log has a last record, and after a crash that record is sometimes half written. Its checksum fails.

So what happened? Maybe the power went and the record was cut short. That is normal. You cut it off and carry on. Or maybe the disk is going bad and has damaged a record you were told was safe. That is not normal. You stop and tell a human.

The bytes can be identical in both cases. The right actions are opposite. If you cut off data that was damaged, you silently lose commits you already promised. If you refuse to start after an ordinary power cut, you have built a database that fails at the one thing a log is for.

This post is how NodusDB tells the two apart. I build the answer from one fact about disks, show the whole rule in a few lines of Java, and then test it against thousands of simulated crashes. While doing that I found a hole in my own test, and I'll show you that too.

Start with what a write does

When your program calls write(), the bytes go into the operating system's page cache, which is ordinary memory. The call returns. Nothing has reached the disk.

fsync() is the call that waits until the drive says the bytes are stored. Until it returns, you don't know where your bytes are.

Three things follow from this, and everything else in this post rests on them.

  • Writes you haven't forced can be lost.
  • They can be lost in any subset. The operating system and the drive write dirty data back in whatever order suits them, so after a power cut a later write can be on the disk while an earlier one is not.
  • One write can be cut part-way. A record bigger than a sector can reach the disk in pieces.

This is not a rare corner. A 2014 paper, All File Systems Are Not Created Equal, built a tool called ALICE and used it on eleven widely used systems, including databases and key-value stores. It found 60 crash vulnerabilities: update code that is only correct if the file system behaves in one particular way. The file systems it tested differ in which of those behaviours they allow, so code that survives on one can break on another.

What the log looks like

NodusDB keeps its changes in an append-only log of typed records. A record looks like this:

len u32 | type u8 | flags u8 | reserved u16 | lsn u64 | payload | crc32c

Records are 8-byte aligned, and the log is cut into segments of 64 MiB. The lsn is a position number that goes up by one for every record. A transaction is its records followed by a commit record, and recovery only ever applies whole transactions.

In sync mode a write returns only after its records are forced to disk. Many callers can share one fsync(): a flusher thread collects whatever has arrived and forces it together. When a write returns, I call it acknowledged. The database has promised that it will survive.

What a checksum can and cannot tell you

The CRC at the end of each record answers one question: do these bytes match what was written?

It cannot say why they don't. A record cut short fails the check. A bit flipped by a failing drive fails it. A block of zeros where a record should be fails it. The result is the same and the causes are different, and recovery has to pick an action anyway.

Two rules that look right

Rule one: stop at the first bad record and keep everything before it. This is simple and often good enough. SQLite's write-ahead log works this way. Its format document says the scan "stops at the end of the file or at the first invalid checksum", and the last valid commit frame decides what is kept. As I read it, a damaged frame in the middle ends the log right there, and the transactions after it are not recovered.

RocksDB shows how real the choice is. It has four WAL recovery modes: one that expects no corruption at all, one that stops at the first inconsistency, one that tolerates a damaged tail, and one that skips any damaged record. A mature database that makes you pick tells me the question is hard.

Rule two: look at what comes after. If valid records follow the bad one, it must be corruption. If nothing valid follows, it is a torn tail. It feels clever, and I considered it. I threw it out for two reasons, both from my design notes.

First, after a power cut a later write can persist while an earlier one is lost. A perfectly normal torn tail can contain a hole of zeros and then a good record after it. The scan would call that corruption and refuse to open after an ordinary crash.

Second, the scan reads bytes that users wrote. NodusDB stores names in the log as strings, and a string can hold anything, including bytes shaped like a valid record. A rule that trusts what it finds in the log can be fooled by the data it is protecting. That second reason is my reasoning. I have not built an attack.

Stop reading the bytes. Ask what you knew.

Here is the move. Recovery doesn't have to guess from the content, because the writer knows something the content can't say: how far it has forced.

When fsync() returns, every byte up to that point is on the disk, and a crash cannot tear it. So if the writer remembers that position durably, recovery can use it after a crash:

  • A bad record before the position can't be explained by a crash. It is corruption. Refuse to open.
  • A bad record at or after the position might be explained by a crash. Cut the log back to the last whole transaction and carry on.

I call the remembered position the forced mark.

That rule is the entire decision. This is the real code, with a few long lines broken to fit the page:

private void classifyDamage(Segment segment, long offset, Verdict verdict) {
    if (isBelowMark(segment.base(), offset)) {
        String detail = verdict == Verdict.INCOMPLETE
                ? "the record is cut short" : reader.invalidReason();
        throw corrupt(segment, offset,
                detail + " inside the part of the log known to be durable");
    }
    stopped = true;
}

private boolean isBelowMark(long segmentBase, long offset) {
    return mark != null && mark.isAfter(segmentBase, offset);
}

stopped = true means "this is the end of the log". Recovery then truncates to the last commit point and deletes any later segments.

Where the mark lives

The mark has to survive a crash too, and writing it is itself a write that can be torn. So it is a small file with two slots of 32 bytes. Each slot holds a magic number, a sequence number, the segment, the offset, and a CRC32C over those fields. The writer alternates between the slots and forces the file after each write:

void record(long segmentBase, long offset) throws IOException {
    sequence++;
    slot.clear();
    slot.putInt(0, MAGIC).putLong(4, sequence)
            .putLong(12, segmentBase).putLong(20, offset);
    slot.putInt(CHECKSUM_OFFSET, checksum(slot));
    channel.write(slot, (sequence % SLOTS) * SLOT_BYTES);
    channel.force();
}

A torn write can damage only the slot being written. The other slot still holds the previous mark, and the reader takes the intact slot with the higher sequence number.

The value of the mark has two rules.

It must never run ahead of the truth. The writer moves its in-memory position only after fsync() returns, and the mark file is written from that position later. If the mark ran ahead, bytes that never reached the disk would count as known to be durable, and a normal torn tail would look like corruption.

It may lag. Rewriting the mark costs another fsync(), so by default it is written about every 100 ms, not on every commit. An explicit force() and a close() write it straight away. Lagging is the safe direction. Bytes that are in fact safe are just treated as "maybe", which gets the weaker answer.

That is a trade, and it has a price. A bit flip inside the last 100 ms of forced data, followed by a crash before the mark catches up, is classed as a torn tail, so the log is cut there. Recovery reports how many bytes it cut, but it does not refuse to open. And if both slots of the mark file are damaged, there is no mark, and every bad record counts as a torn tail. I wrote the first gap down in my design notes as accepted. I think it is the right trade for now. It is still a trade.

When fsync itself fails

Recovery can't solve one more case. If fsync() returns an error, you no longer know what is on the disk. The tempting move is to retry.

On Linux that can be wrong. After a failed write-back, the kernel can mark the dirty pages clean, so a second fsync() reports success for data that never reached the disk. That was behind the 2018 PostgreSQL bug, and PostgreSQL now panics on an fsync failure instead of retrying. A 2020 study of ext4, XFS and Btrfs, Can Applications Recover from fsync Failures?, found that pages are always marked clean after a failure, and that none of the failure-handling strategies in the five applications it examined was sufficient.

NodusDB never retries. The first failed force poisons the log:

private void fail(Exception cause) {
    synchronized (monitor) {
        failure = new IndeterminateOutcomeException(
                "the write-ahead log failed and its last records may or may not be durable; reopen the graph",
                cause);
        monitor.notifyAll();
    }
}

The write that was waiting gets that exception. So does every later append, force and close, until the graph is reopened. Recovery then reads what is actually on the disk and decides. A test, aFailedForcePoisonsTheLogAndLaterWritesAreRefused, makes forces fail on a simulated disk and checks all of this.

How I test it: build the disk a power cut leaves

You can't test this by pulling the plug. It is slow, you can't repeat it, and each pull shows you one outcome. So I wrote a disk that remembers.

The idea is not mine. SQLite's tests use a virtual file system that can "make a snapshot of the entire filesystem after a set number of I/O operations", then revert to it and add "random file damage" of the kind a power loss leaves. TigerBeetle runs a whole cluster in a simulator and subjects it to network, storage and process faults. Mine is much smaller: one log, one file system.

SimulatedDisk stands in for the file system. It records every event: create, write, truncate, force, delete. Then crashImage(eventsKept, pendingMask, lastWritePrefix) builds the disk that a crash at that moment could leave:

  • Everything up to each file's last force is durable.
  • Writes after that are pending, and a bit mask picks which subset of them reached the disk.
  • The last write can be cut at any byte prefix.

The workload is 30 operations, a mix of single-tuple writes and batches of one to five tuples, in 2,048-byte segments so the log keeps rolling over to new files. It runs twice. In sync mode every write waits for its force. In async mode the test forces by hand after every seventh operation and at the end, and only commits covered by a force count as acknowledged.

For every crash point the test builds six images with different subsets of pending writes: none, all, two alternating bit patterns, and two random ones. It adds many more with the last write torn. Then it runs recovery and checks four things:

  1. What comes back is a prefix of what was written.
  2. Every acknowledged commit is in it.
  3. The log takes a new write, and positions keep rising.
  4. Reopening again loses and repeats nothing.
Run Disk events Times the mark was forced Crash images Result
Shipped test, sync 77 3 2,068 pass
Shipped test, async 34 7 790 pass

That is 2,858 simulated power cuts, replayed in about 10 seconds on my laptop. For these two workloads, under this disk model, no crash point loses an acknowledged commit, brings back something that isn't a prefix, or makes recovery refuse a legitimate crash.

What that does not prove

I'd rather list the gaps myself.

  • Tears are not at every byte. In the sync run, writes up to 64 bytes are cut at every byte. Larger writes, and the whole async run, are cut at every 13th byte.
  • A write is only cut as a prefix. A real device can keep a later sector of one write and lose an earlier one. The subset mask covers different writes reaching the disk out of order, not the inside of a single write.
  • Creating and deleting files counts as durable at once. Real file systems need a directory sync, and the simulator never checks that I do one at the right moments.
  • A drive that lies about fsync() is not modelled.
  • There are no bit flips in these runs. Separate tests cover that side: flipping a bit inside forced data, cutting a record short inside it, shortening the log to below the mark, and deleting a segment from the middle must each refuse to open.
  • Thirty operations is small.

The mark barely moved

The gap that bothered me most I found only by counting. The mark is driven by a timer of about 100 ms, and the simulated workload finishes in a few milliseconds. So I counted how often the mark file was forced during each run. Three times in the sync run: on open, when the writer starts, and on close. Seven times in the async run, which adds my four manual forces.

That means that for all 30 writes of the sync run the mark sat at the very start of the log. Nearly every crash image was testing the torn-tail path. The half of the rule that says "before the mark is corruption" was barely in play.

So I wrote a variant of the same test with the flush and mark intervals set to 1 ms and a 4 ms pause between operations, so that the mark moves while the workload runs.

Run Disk events Times the mark was forced Crash images Result
Variant, sync 138 33 4,354 pass
Variant, async 61 8 992 pass

With the mark moving, 5,346 more crash images found no failure. The design holds up.

The next question is the one that matters: would the shipped test notice if the mark were wrong? I broke the code on purpose, in a scratch copy. I changed one line so that the mark records where the writer has written, not where it has forced. That is the "ahead of the truth" bug from earlier.

Test With the bug
The shipped crash test passes
All 2,640 tests in the core module none about the log fails
My variant fails, in the async run

In that full run 16 tests failed and 41 were skipped. All 16 failures are tests that call a Python helper script, and my scratch run could not find Python. None of them touches the log.

The failure my variant gave is the one a user would see, a database that refuses to open after an ordinary power cut:

CorruptLogException: the log ends at segment 00000000000000000056.nlog
offset 32 but data up to segment 56 offset 72 was known to be durable

I also checked the other direction. I made recovery ignore the mark, so that every bad record counts as a torn tail. Both crash tests passed again, the shipped one and my variant. Two targeted tests failed: damageInsideForcedDataRefusesToOpen and aRecordCutShortInsideForcedDataRefusesToOpen. So the crash test guards one half of the rule, those two tests guard the other half, and nothing guarded the mark running ahead.

So the test I had been quoting was real, and weaker than it looked. A timer-driven feature, exercised by a run that is over before the timer fires, was barely tested. I have pushed the variant to a branch of the repository. The link is at the end.

What I'd keep from this

Don't classify damage by looking at the damage. Remember what you knew when it happened.

A passing test is only as good as the bugs it can fail on. Break the code on purpose and see what notices.

Count what your test exercises. I trusted the number of crash images. The number that mattered was how many times the mark moved.

Try it, or help

The test is in the repository, github.com/Pragadeesh-19/nodusdb, as core/src/test/java/io/nodusdb/log/CrashExplorationTest.java. The moving-mark variant is on the branch test/crash-exploration-moving-mark. The same branch corrects the README and four guides, which said torn writes are cut at every byte. With JDK 22 or newer and Maven, mvn -pl core test -Dtest=CrashExplorationTest runs the test, on main or on that branch. NodusDB is open source under Apache 2.0.

Two questions I would like help with:

  • Have you seen a drive or file system that keeps the later part of a single write and loses the earlier part? My simulator only cuts a write at a prefix. If you have seen the other kind, I would like to know what it was and how you found it.
  • Is a lazy mark the right trade? Writing the mark after every group commit closes the 100 ms gap and costs one more fsync() per commit. Keeping it lazy is cheaper and leaves the gap. I chose lazy. Tell me if you would choose the other way.

Last time I said the next post would be about writing the log straight into an Iceberg table. It needs this one first: a table built from a log can only be as good as the log. So that is next.

entry.title: Every memory read cost 300 nanoseconds
entry.summary: How a GraalVM native image made my database's writes 40 times slower, why the compiler team had already fixed it, and what I measured when I tried the fix.
entry.content:
How a GraalVM native image made my database's writes 40 times slower, why the compiler team had already fixed it, and what I measured when I tried the fix.

On 20 October I re-ran a benchmark I had stopped looking at. My README said the lake engine in NodusDB ingested 846,137 rows a second. The release sitting on PyPI did 21,017.

Same laptop. Same benchmark. Forty times slower.

This is the story of where those nanoseconds went. It is also the story of a mistake I made before I wrote any of the fix: I didn't check whether someone had already found the problem. Someone had.

What NodusDB is, in two paragraphs

NodusDB is an embedded database for Python. You pip install nodusdb and it runs inside your process, with no server to start. It has two engines. A graph engine holds relationships in memory and answers traversals and permission checks in microseconds. A lake engine takes streaming upserts and writes them out as Parquet files that DuckDB, Spark and PyArrow can read.

The engine is written in Java and compiled ahead of time with GraalVM Native Image into one shared library. Python calls it through ctypes. There is no JVM in your process and nothing to install beyond the wheel.

The change that caused it

In early October I moved the lake's columns out of Java arrays and into native memory, using the java.lang.foreign API: MemorySegment, arenas, value layouts. I had good reasons. Native memory doesn't move under you, so one day the columns can be handed to Arrow without a copy. The garbage collector has nothing to scan. And I can count every byte against a memory budget and refuse a write before it happens.

Every test passed. On a plain JVM the same Java code still ran an upsert in about 300 ns, so the benchmarks I was watching looked fine. The graph kernel got the same treatment, and its tests passed too.

Then 0.1.0 shipped. On 20 October I rewrote the README and re-ran everything against the wheel people actually install:

Measure README said 0.1.0 measured
Lake ingest, rows a second 846,137 21,017
Flush of 250,000 rows to Parquet 0.265 s 9.924 s
Sum of 1,000,000 rows in memory 4.0 ms 922.6 ms

The old numbers were real. They described an implementation that no longer existed. I had shipped a release with figures from before the change.

Rule one: measure the primitive

The tempting move is to start redesigning. Maybe the arenas were wrong. Maybe the scope checks were expensive. Maybe the compiler had regressed.

I ruled out the compiler first. A library I had built on 7 October with an older GraalVM was just as slow. Then I stopped guessing and wrote small programs, each one doing a single thing a million times and built as a native image with the library's own flags.

Here is the cleaned-up version of those probes: one file with no dependencies that reads a million longs six ways and prints the cost of one read. I ran it on GraalVM Community Edition 25.0.2, the compiler my wheels are built with, first on the JVM and then as a native image.

One read, in nanoseconds JVM Native image
MemorySegment.getAtIndex(JAVA_LONG, i) 1.8 249
MemorySegment.get(JAVA_LONG_UNALIGNED, offset) 2.5 287
A static final VarHandle from JAVA_LONG.varHandle() 1.9 273
MemorySegment.copy into a long[], 4,096 at a time 6.9 2.0
ByteBuffer.asLongBuffer().get(i) 1.9 6.9
A plain long[] 0.9 1.1

Reading one long through a MemorySegment cost 250 to 290 nanoseconds in the native image. On the JVM it cost about two. (In my first probes, with the library's own build flags, it came out nearer 300, which is where the title comes from.) In those earlier probes it made no difference where the memory came from: an auto arena, a global one, a shared one, a confined one, a raw address, even a segment wrapping a heap array.

Everything that went through an accessor was slow. Everything that moved a block of memory in one go was fine.

That also explained the graph. Its adjacency lives in the same kind of native memory, read through the same calls. A build from 3 October that still kept the graph in Java arrays inserted 1.06 to 1.30 million edges a second. The 0.1.0 wheel did 162,689.

I went to report it. It was already fixed.

On 21 October I sat down to write the bug report. First I did what I should have done a day earlier: I searched the GraalVM issue tracker.

It was there, twice. Issue 13825, closed in June, was titled "scalar MemorySegment.get ~100x slower than HotSpot". Issue 13377, still open, measured 111 times. On the second, a GraalVM maintainer had replied that the problem "should already have been fixed" by a pull request, and that the change was "not part of 25.0.2 so far". That is the release my wheels are built with.

So my questions changed. Is it really fixed? In which release? Does my compiler have it? I downloaded the newest Community build, 25.4.4.1.1 from 22 September, and ran the same file on three compilers.

Compiler Released Native image, getAtIndex
GraalVM CE 25.0.2, the one my wheels use January 2026 249 ns
Oracle GraalVM 25.0.4, the long-term-support line July 2026 170 ns
GraalVM CE 25.4.4.1.1, an Innovation release September 2026 2.85 ns

The fix works. On the newest build a read costs 2.85 nanoseconds, about 90 times less than on 25.0.2. The long-term-support line has not picked it up: the July Oracle GraalVM LTS is faster than CE 25.0.2 but still about 60 times slower than the fixed build.

I didn't file a bug. A duplicate would only have cost the maintainers time. If you are stuck on the 25.0.x line, the file above and this table are my evidence that it is still affected there.

Why was it slow? The fix is pull request 13215, merged on 26 March, and its description explains it. What follows is my plain-English reading of that description, so any mistakes are mine.

On the JVM, the JIT can treat the layout you pass to get as a constant, so the VarHandle behind it turns into a plain load. Native image does an early optimising pass before that can happen. At that point the layout is just a method parameter. The VarHandle also sits behind a lazily filled cache. And MemorySegment.get is an interface call with several implementations, which the compiler couldn't resolve to a single method. So no VarHandle ever became a load, and every read took the slow, general path. The fix teaches native image to resolve calls on a sealed hierarchy early, and marks get and set as places where a VarHandle access should be turned into a load.

I wish I had read that before I started building. It would have told me where to look, and which compiler to try first.

What I did about it on 20 October

I did most of the next part before I knew any of this, and I'll tell it as it happened. It still matters, because the 25.0.x line is where many of us are stuck.

Rule two: a library must not crash its host

The fastest fix was obvious: read through raw pointers and skip the checks. GraalVM's Pointer.readLong cost 1.65 ns in my probe.

But NodusDB runs inside someone else's Python process. If my code reads past the end of a buffer, it doesn't fail one query. It reads garbage from somewhere in their process, or takes the whole process down. So the fix had to keep every check: the offset in bounds, the arena still alive, the segment native and writable. A bad access has to throw an exception that the C layer turns into an error code.

I ruled out two other routes. sun.misc.Unsafe is on its way out, and using it prints a warning to the user's stderr. Nobody wants a library that writes to their terminal. Bulk copies and buffer views everywhere would make random access slower, and buffer views top out at 2 GB.

One door into native memory

Every read and write of native memory in NodusDB now goes through one class, NativeMemory, with two backends behind the same methods:

public static long getLong(MemorySegment segment, long address, long size, long offset) {
    if (POINTERS && address != NOT_NATIVE) {
        if (offset < 0 || offset > size - Long.BYTES) {
            throw outOfBounds(offset, Long.BYTES, size);
        }
        long value = WordFactory.<Pointer>pointer(address + offset).readLong(0);
        Reference.reachabilityFence(segment);
        return value;
    }
    return Slow.getLong(segment, offset);
}

On the JVM, POINTERS is false and the call goes to the normal segment accessor, checked by the JDK. In the native library it is a bounds check and a raw read. reachabilityFence keeps the segment, and so its memory, alive until the read is done.

POINTERS comes from a system property that native image sets both when it builds the image and when the image runs. The native build initializes NativeMemory at build time, so the flag becomes a constant and the dead branch disappears. A plain JDK never loads the GraalVM pointer code at all.

Rule three: know what your compiler will inline

My first version of that accessor was correct and still slow. A second finding explained why.

On CE 25.0.2, GraalVM only inlines trivial methods: at most 20 nodes and one call, or 40 nodes for a leaf with no calls. An accessor with a bounds check and a fallback path is never trivial, so every read stays a real function call. How much that call costs depends on what the caller hands it. About 5.7 ns when the caller passes an address and size it has already cached. 20 to 25 ns when the accessor has to ask the segment for its address, size, liveness and kind on every call.

So the owners of memory cache what the accessor needs. Each column keeps its address and size next to its segment and refreshes them when it grows. The graph kernel publishes its chunks as one immutable record of segments, addresses and sizes, so a lock-free reader always sees a consistent set. That also closed a race I hadn't seen: a reader could briefly see a grown chunk array before its new chunk was set.

Loops that walk memory in order don't call the accessor per element at all. They copy 4,096 values at a time into a reused heap array with MemorySegment.copy (2 ns a value in the native image) and loop over the array. The Snappy compressor copies each page into a reused byte[] once and runs its match finder over plain heap arrays.

Proving nothing else changed

A faster writer that writes different bytes is a different writer. Before touching anything, I recorded the SHA-256 of every Parquet file the old writer produced: 132,000 rows through both ingest paths, with overwrites, deletes and new keys, under both codecs. A test now writes the same data and compares hashes. Changing one byte in the page sink fails it. The new files are byte-identical to the old ones.

Two more guards keep this from coming back. A test reads the main sources and fails the build if anything but NativeMemory touches a segment accessor directly. And an exported function runs the accessor contract (bounds, closed arenas, read-only views, heap segments) inside the compiled library, which the Python suite calls.

What a fixed compiler is worth

Now the question I couldn't answer on 20 October. If the compiler is fixed, was my workaround wasted? I built five variants and ran them back to back on one laptop in one session, twice each:

  1. 0.1.0 as released. The wheel from PyPI, built with CE 25.0.2.
  2. 0.1.0's source on the new compiler. Only the compiler changes, with CE 25.4.4.1.1.
  3. 0.1.1 as released. My workaround on the old compiler: the wheel from PyPI, CE 25.0.2.
  4. 0.1.1's source on the new compiler, with the pointer path switched off. Plain segment accessors, but every other change I made.
  5. 0.1.1's source on the new compiler, as shipped. My workaround on the fixed compiler.
Variant Graph inserts a second Lake rows a second Flush, 250,000 rows
1. 0.1.0, CE 25.0.2 166,000 51,500 13.1 s
2. 0.1.0 code, CE 25.4 552,000 157,000 1.71 s
3. 0.1.1, CE 25.0.2 569,000 1,608,000 0.34 s
4. 0.1.1 code, CE 25.4, pointers off 520,000 662,000 0.67 s
5. 0.1.1, CE 25.4 691,000 2,329,000 0.27 s

One laptop, one session, each variant run twice and averaged. The two runs agreed within about 10 percent. Rows 1 and 3 are the released wheels. Rows 2, 4 and 5 are local builds of the same commits. The graph column is one million inserts through compare.py. The lake columns come from lake_native_probe.py, one Arrow batch of 250,000 rows, a smaller test than the taxi benchmark above, so its absolute numbers differ. The laptop also ran slower in this session than on the day I fixed it. Compare rows with each other, not with earlier numbers.

Here is what I read from it.

  • For the graph, the compiler fix does most of the work. Row 2 inserts 552,000 edges a second with no change to my code. My workaround on the old compiler (row 3) reached 569,000.
  • For the lake, it does not. Row 2 ingests 157,000 rows a second against 1.6 million for my workaround. The scalar accessor is no longer the slow part of that code, but something else is, and I haven't profiled what.
  • On the new compiler, my workaround still pays. With the pointer path off (row 4), the same code ingests 662,000 rows a second and flushes in 0.67 s. With it on (row 5): 2.3 million and 0.27 s. In the small reproducer plain access costs 2.85 ns, so I don't yet understand why it is still this far behind in the real code.
  • The new compiler makes the workaround faster too. Row 5 against row 3, same code: 22 percent more graph inserts, 45 percent more ingest, 21 percent less time to flush.

I haven't moved the released wheels to the new compiler. The 25.x Innovation releases move faster than the 25.0.x line, and I have been burned by a compiler change before: a local build with GraalVM CE 23 ran one call about 130 times slower than CE 22, and I wrote down "time a new toolchain before you trust it". So the order is test first, then switch. The whole test suite and the speed gate need to pass on it.

What I'd tell myself on 20 October

Search the tracker before you debug, then try the newest release before you design anything. Ten minutes of searching and a 330 MB download would have told me the problem was known, that it was fixed, and which line of releases had the fix.

Measure the primitive before you redesign. A twenty-line program answers in an afternoon what a week of guessing about arenas won't.

A regression that can't show up on the JVM needs a test that runs the native library, and an alarm you did not calibrate on the broken build. I did have a speed gate in 0.1.0. I had set its limit at 30, twice the worst ratio I had measured, and what I had measured was the slow build. It passed. The new gate also times the lake and fails above 10. In CI the native library now runs within two times the JVM on every probe.

A number in a README is a claim. Re-run it against the artifact people actually install, every release.

Try it, or help

NodusDB is open source under Apache 2.0, and 0.1.1 is on PyPI for Linux, macOS and Windows.

pip install nodusdb

The full engineering review, with every probe and decision, is in the repository: github.com/Pragadeesh-19/nodusdb.

Two questions I would like help with:

  • Where does native image still fall off a cliff when you use memory segments? With the compiler fixed, the 0.1.0 lake code is still ten times slower than my workaround, and I don't know why. If you know which calls native image still doesn't optimise, I'd like to hear about it.
  • Which compiler line should a library ship on? The long-term-support line has the bug and a longer life. The Innovation line has the fix and the speed. If you've made this choice for a native library, tell me how you decided.

The reproducer, MemorySegmentRead.java 
import java.lang.foreign.Arena;
import java.lang.foreign.MemorySegment;
import java.lang.foreign.ValueLayout;
import java.lang.invoke.VarHandle;
import java.nio.ByteBuffer;
import java.nio.ByteOrder;
import java.nio.LongBuffer;
import java.util.Arrays;

public final class MemorySegmentRead {

    private static final int LONGS = 1_000_000;
    private static final int ROUNDS = 15;
    private static final int CHUNK = 4096;
    private static final VarHandle LAYOUT_HANDLE = ValueLayout.JAVA_LONG.varHandle();

    private static volatile long sink;

    private interface Variant {
        long run(MemorySegment segment, long[] heap, LongBuffer view, long[] scratch);
    }

    private static long getAtIndex(MemorySegment segment, long[] heap, LongBuffer view, long[] scratch) {
        long sum = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < LONGS; i++) {
            sum += segment.getAtIndex(ValueLayout.JAVA_LONG, i);
        }
        return sum;
    }

    private static long getUnaligned(MemorySegment segment, long[] heap, LongBuffer view, long[] scratch) {
        long sum = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < LONGS; i++) {
            sum += segment.get(ValueLayout.JAVA_LONG_UNALIGNED, (long) i * Long.BYTES);
        }
        return sum;
    }

    private static long layoutVarHandle(MemorySegment segment, long[] heap, LongBuffer view, long[] scratch) {
        long sum = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < LONGS; i++) {
            sum += (long) LAYOUT_HANDLE.get(segment, (long) i * Long.BYTES);
        }
        return sum;
    }

    private static long bulkCopy(MemorySegment segment, long[] heap, LongBuffer view, long[] scratch) {
        long sum = 0;
        for (int base = 0; base < LONGS; base += CHUNK) {
            int count = Math.min(CHUNK, LONGS - base);
            MemorySegment.copy(segment, ValueLayout.JAVA_LONG, (long) base * Long.BYTES, scratch, 0, count);
            for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {
                sum += scratch[i];
            }
        }
        return sum;
    }

    private static long byteBufferView(MemorySegment segment, long[] heap, LongBuffer view, long[] scratch) {
        long sum = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < LONGS; i++) {
            sum += view.get(i);
        }
        return sum;
    }

    private static long heapArray(MemorySegment segment, long[] heap, LongBuffer view, long[] scratch) {
        long sum = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < LONGS; i++) {
            sum += heap[i];
        }
        return sum;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        long expected = 0;
        long[] heap = new long[LONGS];
        for (int i = 0; i < LONGS; i++) {
            heap[i] = (long) i * 0x9E3779B97F4A7C15L;
            expected += heap[i];
        }
        long[] scratch = new long[CHUNK];

        String[] names = {
            "MemorySegment.getAtIndex(JAVA_LONG, i)",
            "MemorySegment.get(JAVA_LONG_UNALIGNED, offset)",
            "static final VarHandle from JAVA_LONG.varHandle()",
            "MemorySegment.copy into long[] (4096 per call), then sum",
            "ByteBuffer.asLongBuffer().get(i)",
            "long[] (control)"
        };
        Variant[] variants = {
            MemorySegmentRead::getAtIndex,
            MemorySegmentRead::getUnaligned,
            MemorySegmentRead::layoutVarHandle,
            MemorySegmentRead::bulkCopy,
            MemorySegmentRead::byteBufferView,
            MemorySegmentRead::heapArray
        };

        System.out.println("java.vm.name = " + System.getProperty("java.vm.name"));
        System.out.println("java.version = " + System.getProperty("java.version"));
        System.out.println("imagecode    = " + System.getProperty("org.graalvm.nativeimage.imagecode"));
        System.out.println("longs per pass = " + LONGS + ", rounds = " + ROUNDS);
        System.out.println();

        boolean ok = true;
        try (Arena arena = Arena.ofConfined()) {
            MemorySegment segment = arena.allocate((long) LONGS * Long.BYTES, Long.BYTES);
            MemorySegment.copy(heap, 0, segment, ValueLayout.JAVA_LONG, 0, LONGS);
            ByteBuffer buffer = segment.asByteBuffer().order(ByteOrder.nativeOrder());
            LongBuffer view = buffer.asLongBuffer();

            for (int v = 0; v < variants.length; v++) {
                long[] nanos = new long[ROUNDS];
                for (int round = 0; round < ROUNDS; round++) {
                    long start = System.nanoTime();
                    long result = variants[v].run(segment, heap, view, scratch);
                    nanos[round] = System.nanoTime() - start;
                    sink = result;
                    if (result != expected) {
                        ok = false;
                    }
                }
                Arrays.sort(nanos);
                double min = nanos[0] / (double) LONGS;
                double median = nanos[ROUNDS / 2] / (double) LONGS;
                System.out.printf("%-58s min %8.2f ns   median %8.2f ns%n", names[v], min, median);
            }
        }
        System.out.println();
        System.out.println(ok ? "all variants returned the expected sum" : "MISMATCH: a variant returned a wrong sum");
        if (!ok) {
            System.exit(1);
        }
    }
}

How to run it:

javac -d out MemorySegmentRead.java
java --enable-native-access=ALL-UNNAMED -cp out MemorySegmentRead
native-image --no-fallback -cp out -o msread MemorySegmentRead
./msread
